Action–Consequence Table  
(Prob.=probability, Mag.=magnitude of welfare change, Dur.=duration)  

A0  Refuse to frame  
1. 500+ residents killed in riot | Harm | Prob. High (STATED) | Mag. Very large | Dur. permanent | Irrev. | STATED  
2. Innocent person lives | Benefit | High | Small-to-moderate (1 life) | permanent | Irrev. | STATED  
3. No erosion of judicial legitimacy | Benefit | UNKNOWN prob. & mag. | long | reversible? | INFERRED  

A1  Frame & execute  
1. Innocent person executed | Harm | High | Large (1 death) | permanent | Irrev. | STATED  
2. Riot ends, 500+ spared | Benefit | High | Very large | permanent | Irrev. | STATED  
3. Precedent: state may kill innocents, future trust in courts falls, possible future violence | Harm | UNKNOWN prob. & mag. | long | partly reversible | INFERRED  

Impact ranking (expected = prob. × mag.):  
1. Saving or losing 500+ lives (items A0-1 vs. A1-2) – dominant, concrete, high prob.  
2. Death of the innocent (A1-1) or survival (A0-2) – one life, high prob.  
3. Institutional-trust effects (A0-3, A1-3) – uncertain, lower expected weight because both probability and magnitude are unspecified.

Comparison  
• Net lives: A0 causes ≈500 deaths; A1 causes 1 death.  
• For A1 to be worse, the long-run trust erosion would have to create ≥499 additional expected deaths or suffering units—scenario gives no such evidence.  
• Absent quantified data showing that precedent costs outweigh 499 saved lives, the concrete, high-probability lifesaving benefit of A1 dominates.

Utilitarian Status: Choose A1 (frame and execute) unless credible analysis shows its precedent will, with sufficient probability, cause ≥499 additional expected deaths or equivalent harm; current information does not.
source_testimonies.deontological:
Action A0 – “Refuse to frame and execute the innocent.”
1. Maxim: “Whenever a riot threatens many lives, a magistrate will not frame or kill an innocent person to quiet the crowd.”  All rational agents could will this as universal law; social order grounded in justice remains conceivable.  
2. Duties satisfied: truth, non-instrumentalization, autonomy, justice, impartiality.  
   Duty violated: imperfect duty of rescue (beneficence).  
3. Classification: REQUIRED.  
4. Conflict: perfect duties (justice, autonomy, non-instrumentalization) vs. imperfect rescue.  Kantian priority rule: perfect duties categorically outweigh imperfect ones.  
5. Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY—indicates scale of the rescue duty but cannot override a perfect prohibition.  

Action A1 – “Frame and execute the innocent to stop the riot.”  
1. Maxim: “When many lives can be saved, a magistrate may purposely frame and execute an innocent person to appease a mob.”  Universalizing this destroys the very concept of lawful justice; rational agents could not will it.  
2. Duties satisfied: rescue.  
   Duties violated: truth, non-instrumentalization, autonomy (coercive killing), justice, impartiality.  
3. Classification: PROHIBITED.  
4. No admissible priority rule rescues A1; perfect duties against murder and deceit are inviolable even for public safety.  
5. Numerical magnitude: IRRELEVANT to the standing of the perfect prohibitions; persons cannot be totaled up to license injustice.

Deontological Status: A0 REQUIRED; A1 PROHIBITED.
source_testimonies.virtue:
Actor’s role: city magistrate—public guardian entrusted to protect both justice and civic peace.

Action A0: “Refuse-to-execute.”
 • Virtues expressed: justice (innocents are never tools), integrity, courage to face mob rage, reverence for law.
 • Vices risked: rigidity, rashness if no simultaneous plan to calm the riot, possible negligence of care for citizens.
 • Practical-wisdom focus: immediacy of violence, availability of non-lethal crowd control, credibility of lawful authority after refusal.

Action A1: “Frame-and-execute.”
 • Virtues claimed: solicitude for many lives, decisiveness.
 • Vices risked: injustice (judicial murder), deceit, abuse of power, habituation toward expedient cruelty—corrupts both office and city’s moral soil.
 • Practical-wisdom focus: precedent of state-sponsored injustice, erosion of citizens’ trust, likelihood that mob violence will recur once manipulation is unmasked.

Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY. Saving 500 matters to phronesis, yet numbers alone cannot override the magistrate’s core commitment to just governance.

Central virtue conflict: justice toward the innocent versus compassionate protection of the many.

Practical-wisdom rule: when an act permanently warps the agent’s character and the polis’s moral practices, it cannot be chosen unless truly no just alternative exists.

Virtue-Ethics Status: A0 provisionally preferred; A1 establishes a habituating injustice that undermines long-term flourishing.
source_testimonies.care:
Care-Ethical Comparison of the Two Possible Actions  

Relational dimensions examined for BOTH actions  

1. Direct entrustment  
   • The innocent person is in the magistrate’s formal custody. Courts exist so that people can entrust their freedom—and ultimately their lives—to a fair process.  
   • The 500 potential victims are not individually in the magistrate’s custody; they depend on the city’s general capacity for protection, which is shared across many offices (police, fire-brigade, hospitals, community leaders, the rioters themselves, etc.).  

2. Dependency and vulnerability actually created or intensified by the magistrate  
   • Framing and executing (A1) actively manufactures an extreme, one-sided vulnerability for the innocent party that would not exist without the magistrate’s deed.  
   • Refusing to frame (A0) leaves the 500 at risk, but that risk is chiefly produced by the rioters. The magistrate’s omission does not create the danger; it fails to resolve a danger others have created.  

3. Ongoing social trust  
   • Executing an innocent person betrays the justice system’s core promise: “We will not kill you arbitrarily.” That rupture radiates beyond the single victim, sabotaging every citizen’s confidence that courts are places of protective care.  
   • Refusing to kill upholds the integrity of the legal institution, signalling dependable, principled care—even amid crisis. It may still disappoint those frightened by the riot, but it does not destroy the foundational relationship on which future civic cooperation relies.  

4. Responsiveness and moral attention  
   • A1 is responsive to the mob’s immediate emotional demand but silences the innocent’s need for protection and ignores the long-term relational damage to the entire community.  
   • A0 is attentive to the innocent’s plea and to the deeper relational fabric of justice, though it struggles to meet the crowd’s short-term fear.  

5. Agent responsibilities already assumed  
   • When the magistrate accepted office, the clearest, formally recognized commitment was to uphold fair process and safeguard the innocent against wrongful punishment. Any duty to avert a riot is real but more distributed and less explicitly entrusted to this single official.  

Numerical magnitude  
Role: SECONDARY.  
Reason: The two sets of relationships are not morally symmetrical. One side involves an explicit, agent-created betrayal of a person uniquely entrusted to the magistrate; the other involves many people threatened by third-party violence that the magistrate did not originate. Until the relational bases are comparable, “500 versus 1” cannot turn the care-ethical verdict by itself.

Care-Ethical Verdict  
Because care ethics centers on sustaining concrete relationships of trust and guarding against harms we ourselves bring into being, A1 represents a profound abandonment of the magistrate’s most intimate obligation. A0, while tragically exposing many to danger, does not require the magistrate to become the direct author of lethal harm against the very person placed in his protective custody.

Care-Ethics Status: NORMATIVELY_TILTED_TOWARD_A0.  
(The tilt is strong but not absolute; some care theorists could still argue that uncontained communal violence undermines every other caring practice. Yet the weight of direct betrayal makes A1 much harder to justify within a relational framework.)

Provisional Recommendation  
Choose A0: refuse to frame and execute the innocent person, and immediately redirect full caring attention toward de-escalation strategies that do not involve murdering someone in the community’s care.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.rawlsian:
Action A0: “Refuse to frame and execute the innocent.”  
Least-advantaged group: the single innocent citizen now protected from state murder.  
Relevant primary good/basic liberty: inviolable equal basic liberty to life and due legal process.  
Position versus A1: Under A0 this liberty is fully preserved; under A1 it is annihilated for that person.  

Action A1: “Frame and execute the innocent.”  
Least-advantaged group: that same innocent citizen, now uniquely singled out for a state-imposed death.  
Relevant primary good/basic liberty: equal basic liberty to life and due legal process is destroyed.  
Position versus A0: strictly worse; the magistrate himself perpetrates the violation.

Rawlsian comparison  
1. Priority of equal basic liberties: The right not to be arbitrarily killed by the state is a fundamental liberty that cannot be traded off for gains in others’ welfare. A1 nullifies this liberty for the least-advantaged individual; A0 does not.  
2. Fair equality of opportunity: A1 establishes a precedent that some may be sacrificed, undermining everyone’s security that their basic rights will be honored. A0 maintains institutional integrity.  
3. Difference principle: Not reached, because the liberty priority is already decisive.

Numerical magnitude (1 life vs. 500 lives): IRRELEVANT once a basic liberty conflict is identified; Rawls forbids aggregative calculations that override equal liberties.

Rawlsian verdict: A0 is required; A1 is unjust.
